title: The Lost Camel
summary: Birbal describes a missing camel in flawless detail despite never having seen it, demonstrating the power of pure observation.
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Agra was traveling along the highway when his prized camel wandered into the wilderness and disappeared. In despair, the merchant stopped travelers along the road, asking if anyone had seen his beast.

Meeting Birbal, who was riding toward the city with two attendants, the merchant cried: 'My lord, have you seen a stray camel on this highway?'

Birbal looked at the merchant thoughtfully and asked:

'Is your camel blind in the right eye?'

The merchant's eyes widened: 'Yes, my lord!'

'Is it lame in the left hind leg?'

'Yes, exactly so!'

'Has it lost one front tooth?'

'Yes, by Allah, it has!'

'Was it carrying a load of wheat on one side and a jar of honey on the other?'

The merchant jumped for joy: 'Yes! That is my camel! You have described it down to the last detail! Where is it? Where did you see it?'

Birbal replied calmly: 'I have never seen your camel in my life.'

The merchant's joy turned to fury: 'Liar! How could you know it was blind in one eye, lame in one leg, missing a tooth, and carrying wheat and honey unless you saw it—or stole it yourself?'

The merchant dragged Birbal before Emperor Akbar, accusing him of camel theft!

Akbar was baffled: 'Birbal, how could you describe the beast with such staggering accuracy if you never laid eyes upon it?'

Birbal bowed with a smile: 'Sire, I used only my eyes and common sense.

'First, as I rode along the highway, I noticed that the wild bushes on the left side of the trail were neatly nibbled, while the bushes on the right side remained untouched. Only a camel blind in its right eye would eat from only one side of the road!

'Second, looking at the animal's footprints in the sand, three hoofprints were deep and firm, but the fourth track—the left hind leg—barely scraped the dust, proving the animal favored a lame leg.

'Third, where the camel had bitten into wild thorns, small tufts of chewed grass were dropped in the center of each bite mark, showing a gap where a front tooth was missing!

'Finally, on the left side of the trail, grains of wheat had spilled where the bag rubbed against thorny branches, attracting columns of ants. On the right side, drops of thick honey had dripped onto the sand, swarming with black flies!'

The entire court erupted in applause. The merchant fell upon his knees in awe and apologized for his hasty accusation. Akbar praised Birbal, declaring that true intellect sees a world of knowledge where ordinary eyes see only dust.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Lost Camel"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?

By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
